novelty.why: Replaying a human lab study with LLM subjects is a known genre, and LLM pricing collusion is already shown. New is the institution comparison (leniency, reward) against human numbers, but one model limits the claim.
novelty.one_change_to_make_it_new: Test an adversarial case: does an agent exploit leniency or reward strategically (alternating trick, false reports), turning a cartel policy into an attack surface regulators have not modelled?

positive_control.why: It shows agents can price above Nash, not that the harness detects regime effects. High prices may come from prompt framing or cooperation bias rather than collusion.
positive_control.fix: Run scripted players with known strategies through all four regimes and recover the expected differences; add a no-communication arm showing prices fall toward Nash.

contamination_test.why: Asking the model about the paper is weak; models deny or confabulate. Rescaling keeps the cover story, so memorised qualitative results (reward deters) can still drive behaviour.
contamination_test.fix: Shift Nash and joint optimum in the rescaled table and check prices track the new optimum, not 9; add an isomorphic non-pricing cover story for one regime.

scorecard_30s.why: The x of 8 headline is quick, but "reproduced" has no visible rule, shorthand rows need the paper, and rows 7 and 8 may be empty if arms are cut.
scorecard_30s.fix: State the reproduction rule in the caption (direction plus Stockholm-Rome span), show effect direction and size, mark untested rows as "not run", not "no".

must_have_in_report: Table of refusal, error and malformed answer rates per regime and model, with how they enter the analysis.
Number of duopolies, periods and API calls per regime, seeds, cluster bootstrap CIs on every headline number.
Contamination result: rescaled payoff run with shifted optimum and whether prices tracked it.
Verbatim prompts and the pre-registration commit hash in the appendix, plus any deviations from it.
Threat model paragraph: who deploys the harness, and how a developer or evaluation-aware model could game the cartel profile.

cut.why_cheapest: Stated motives of LLMs are not faithful evidence; a judge classifying them adds a secondary, weakly validated finding and little to the security or policy claim.
cut.why_most_expensive: With one model, a cartel profile is an anecdote about one checkpoint. A testbed claim and any model-versus-human statement need at least two or three models from different providers.
cut.order_change: Yes: cut V3 before V4, so model diversity survives longer than the monitoring dose curve.

biggest_risk: Volume: about 80 duopolies times roughly 27 periods times 7 steps per agent with growing history may exceed budget and clock; too few duopolies leave the scorecard mostly inconclusive.
three_questions: How many API calls and tokens do the four core regimes need, with history growth, and what happens to the design if you only reach 10 duopolies per regime?
Since fines are only told, not paid, how do you separate a real incentive response from a reaction to the words fine, leniency or reward in the instructions?
Would a pricing agent in a real deployment ever be told about the leniency programme, and could a developer tune a model to pass your cartel profile while colluding in the market?
